items.prompt: Move nothing. Black plays 18...Bxf3 19.Bxf3 Rxb5 20.Bxg4 Rxb1 21.Rxb1 (6 plies). Tap every loose piece (attacked and not defended), of either colour, in the position after the last move. Tap nothing if there is none.

claims.statement: After the six moves, the White pieces that are loose are exactly: g4.
After the six moves, the Black pieces that are loose are exactly: none.
After the six moves a White bishop stands on g4.
After the six moves a black knight stands on f6.
After the six moves the black piece on f6 attacks g4.
After the six moves no White piece defends g4.

hints: Start with what left the board: after six plies, which pieces of each side are gone?
The bishop that captured on g4 stopped there. Ask what attacks that square and what defends it.
One piece is loose, and it is the bishop standing on g4.
items.explain: After the six moves the bishop that took on g4 is attacked by the black knight on f6 and no White piece defends it, so it is loose. Nothing else, of either colour, is loose. Updating moved / gone / attacked after each ply gets there without moving a piece.

After the six moves the White knight on f3 attacks d4.

hints: Every move here is a capture or a check. After each one, update: moved, gone, attacked now.
Look at the black knight in the middle of the board. Who attacks it, and who defends it?
The loose piece is the black knight on d4.
items.explain: The knight on d4 is attacked by the knight on f3 and no black piece defends it, so it is loose. It was already loose after the second move, and it is still loose after the queen and rook exchanges that follow. Every move in this line is a capture or a check, so the list changes in obvious ways.

claims.statement: After the six moves, the White pieces that are loose are exactly: none.

hints: The first two moves are 18.Nxf6+ gxf6, after which the knight on d4 is loose. The third move is quiet. Start the list again from there.
After the quiet move, ask what the opponent can capture. Which White piece was doing the attacking?
Black takes the White knight on f3, so d4 loses its attacker. Check each side for any other loose piece.
items.explain: The first two moves are the same as before, and the knight on d4 is loose after them. 19.Qd2 is quiet: no capture, no check. Black answers 19...Bxf3 and takes the White knight that was attacking d4. After 20.Rxe8+ Qxe8 nothing, of either colour, is loose. A picture frozen after the second move (knight on d4 loose) gives the wrong answer here.

items.prompt: White to move. Candidates: A) Ne7+  B) Qxc4  C) Bc1. You can look deeply at one candidate, following its forcing moves to the end, and take a short look at the other two (the opponent's checks, captures and threats after your move). Which candidate gets the deep look, or does none need it?

claims.statement: Ne7+ forces checkmate in 3 or fewer against the engine's best defence (depth 16).
Ne7+ is the engine's best move (depth 16).
Qxc4 is at least 4 pawns worse than the best move (depth 16).
After Qxc4 the mover's net material change along the engine's best defence is at most -2 (depth 16).
After Qxc4 the loose White pieces are exactly: c4.
After Bc1 no material changes hands along the engine's best defence (depth 16).
After Bc1 none of the mover's pieces is loose.

hints: List the forcing moves among the three: which are checks, which are captures?
After each forcing candidate, ask what the opponent can do. Can the piece just be taken for free?
One forcing candidate can be refuted at once; the other keeps its pieces safe and keeps checking.
items.explain: A) Ne7+ gets the deep look: it is a forced mate in three or fewer (engine, depth 16), and the Lichess puzzle solution runs 26.Ne7+ Kh7 27.Qf5+ g6 28.Qxg6#. B) Qxc4 puts the queen where it is attacked and nothing defends it, and loses at least two points of material along the best defence, so a short look settles it. C) Bc1 is quiet: it leaves no White piece loose and no material changes hands along the best defence, so a short look is enough.

items.explain: C) Ng3+ gets the deep look: it is a forced mate in three or fewer (engine, depth 16). B) Rxg2 takes a pawn but the rook is then attacked and nothing defends it, and the engine's best defence leaves Black at least two points down: a short look refutes it. A) Rg8 steps onto g8, where the White knight on f6 attacks it. The king defends it, but a rook for a knight is a loss, and the engine puts Rg8 at least 4 pawns behind the best move (depth 16). A short look at White's captures finds Nxg8.
